transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it's... it's a lot of things, really. I guess the main reason I finally made the appointment is because things at work are just getting out of hand. I've been in construction for twenty years, right out of high school, and I'm a manager now, which means I'm juggling a dozen subcontractors, material deliveries, inspectors, weather delays, you name it. 

But what really brings me in today is that I just cannot keep my head in the game when it matters most. Like, I can start a morning safety briefing with the crew, or sit down in the trailer for a major blueprint and plan review, and I go in trying so hard to pay attention. I really do. I tell myself to just look at the paper, listen to the safety guy, focus on the specs. But I swear, within minutes—literally just a couple of minutes—my mind is completely off on three other job problems. I'll start worrying about whether the concrete trucks are going to get backed up at the south gate, or if the electricians got the right gauge wire for the second floor, or what the drywall guys were complaining about yesterday. 

And because my brain is just bouncing around trying to put out all these other fires, I end up missing things in the review. Important things that I know I should have caught. In my line of work, missing a detail on a structural plan or a safety protocol isn't just a small mistake, it can cost thousands of dollars, or worse, somebody could get seriously hurt. And it's not like I don't care, I care a lot, it's just that the moment I have to sit still and focus on that one document, I'm suddenly trying to solve yesterday's problems and tomorrow's problems all at once, and then the meeting is over and I have to ask my foreman what we just agreed on. It's getting really bad, and I just... I don't know how to stop doing it. I mean, just last week we had this huge pour scheduled and I... well, anyway, it's just a constant struggle to stay locked in.
Looking back, did you experience similar difficulties with focus and attention when you were a child or in school?

Oh, man, school... yeah. If you ask my mom, she'll probably tell you she spent half my childhood sitting in those tiny chairs in the principal's office. 

Even way back in elementary school, like second or third grade, I remember my teachers were already pulling my parents aside at every single parent-teacher conference. They’d always tell them that I just could not stay glued to my seat. Like, I’d be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or I'd wander over to the window because I heard the garbage truck outside, or I'd just be walking around to see what another kid was drawing. It drove my teachers absolutely crazy. 

And the talking... man, my report cards always had those heavy checkmarks next to "talks out of turn." I just had a thought and it had to come out right then, you know? I couldn't hold it in. I'd just blurt out the answer or interrupt the teacher while she was right in the middle of explaining something. I wasn't trying to be disrespectful, it was just like my mouth moved before my brain could hit the brakes.

Then there was the homework situation, which was just a complete disaster. I’d actually do the math worksheet—well, sometimes I did—but then I'd somehow lose it between the kitchen table and my backpack. Or it would get crumpled up at the very bottom of my desk under a bunch of old permission slips, so the teacher thought I just didn't do it. My dad used to get so frustrated trying to help me keep my folders organized, but it just never stuck for more than a day.

And whenever we had in-class assignments, I was always the first one done, but definitely not because I was some kind of genius. I just rushed through the directions before I even really understood what they were asking me to do. I’d look at a worksheet, read the first three words of the instructions, assume I knew what the rest said, and just start scribbling. I'd get half the page wrong just because I missed the part where it said "circle the odd numbers" instead of crossing them out, or whatever it was. It's like my brain was always ten steps ahead of where my eyes actually were on the page. 

So, yeah... looking back, this isn't exactly a new problem for me. It's just that back then, rushing through things or losing a paper meant I got a bad grade on a spelling test. Now, if I lose a paper or rush through reading a spec sheet, it's messing with my livelihood and my crew's safety. But yeah, the teachers were definitely seeing this stuff in me when I was just a little kid.
Nowadays, do you still feel physically restless, fidgety, or like you constantly have an internal motor running?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because... well, no. Not really. Not physically, anyway. I mean, I know I just told you about how I couldn't stay in my seat as a kid, but nowadays? I don't really get that feeling in my body. I don't feel like I have a motor running, or like I need to jump out of my skin if I have to sit still. 

Honestly, it might just be because of the line of work I'm in. I'm on my feet so much out on the site. I mean, a typical Tuesday for me involves walking through thick mud, climbing up three flights of temporary scaffolding to check on the framers, hiking all the way over to the south perimeter to argue with a delivery driver who parked in the wrong unloading zone, and then hauling myself all the way back to the trailer. By the time I actually do sit down in my office chair, my body is just completely beat. I'm forty years old now, and twenty years of walking on hard concrete and wearing heavy steel-toe boots... man, it really does a number on your knees and your lower back, let me tell you. 

So physically, I'm more than happy to just sit still. I don't sit there tapping my foot or fidgeting with my hands or anything like that. I can sit in the cab of my truck for my whole lunch break and barely move a single muscle. It’s just... well, like I was saying earlier, it’s my brain that’s doing all the bouncing around now, not my legs. But as far as feeling physically restless or having some kind of internal motor pushing me to keep moving? No, I haven't really noticed anything like that in a long, long time. I guess I just wear myself out too much during the day for my body to have any extra energy left over to fidget. Like just yesterday, we had this massive lumber delivery and I had to walk the forklift operator through the entire staging area because the ground was too soft from the rain, and by the end of it I was just dragging... so yeah, no physical motor running here.
